title: Duke's vocalists: why they were inferior to his musicians
summary: Procope says Duke had many singers and used them as part of a show and not as stars, hiring none who were already famous.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: What did you think of Duke's various vocalists?

Oh, gee whiz, he had so many vocalists. I remember I asked Tony Watkins, who was Duke's last -- excuse me -- last vocalist, I said, "Tony, how many girl singers has Duke had since you've been the male vocalist?" He said nine. And to my mind Tony was only with the band a short time. You know, comparatively.
So he must have had I don't know how many girl vocalists.

Well, I always found a strange disparity there. I found that very few of his singers matched his musicians, you know, as far as real talent is concerned. I always thought that for the band that it was he had remarkably inferior singers.
Well, now, that's a thing I would say generally that you're right. But I suppose -- I don't know,

but I suppose Duke thought that all he wanted a vocalist to do was sing one or two songs or three or four songs a night. And they didn't have to be Ella Fitzgerald or Sarah Vaughan to sing these songs, because the people that were hearing songs, some of them for the first time, and they probably wouldn't hear them again till the next time they heard Duke's band. And the people who recorded with Duke, if you listen to records, you'll see that Duke recorded them very well. Plus the arrangements that were around these vocalists, you know, that added to it. And the vocalists sang of course, and maybe somebody like Ray Nance would come out and play eight bars and it all added to it. Then the complete thing was there, like a show. You know. It was show business, I think.
But he did some very innovative things in the early days, with Baby Cox, when he had her growling and smiling, you know.
And then it was a big jump, it seems to me, from that -- and then Ivie Anderson, of course. But when he then went to Joya Sherrill and Tony Watkins, you know, it was kind of a letdown.
It just -- it seemed a discrepancy there. I never really understood why that was. But I guess your information is probably right, that he didn't see the vocalist as that --
Their function was a minor function.

The vocalist was just a part of what was going on, not to be a featured singer, not to be a star as such. If, after they came with the band, they became a star, that was something else. But he wasn't going around looking to hire any stars, you know. Like I don't doubt that an Ella Fitzgerald or a Sarah Vaughan or a Lena Horne, somebody like that, you know, after they were a big name, then he'd hire them to sing with the band, you know. Then everybody would say, 'Oh, wow, Lena Horne singing with Duke!' You know. But it wasn't that way.
